parts.instructionsEn: You will hear eight short exchanges. Choose the correct answer for each. Note: some options are true but do not answer the question.

context.transcript:
PART 1 — EIGHT SHORT EXCHANGES

Exchange 1 — Returning a faulty laptop
W: I bought this laptop six weeks ago and the screen keeps flickering. Well — not keeps. It comes and goes, which is almost worse, because when I brought it in your colleague couldn't reproduce it and more or less implied I'd imagined it.
M: Right. I should say that under the returns policy I can only authorise an exchange within thirty days, so strictly speaking we're outside that window.
W: I'm aware of that, and I'm not asking for my money back. I'd simply like it repaired without being told for a third time that there's nothing wrong with it.
M: Then what I'll do is send it to the service centre with a note that the fault is intermittent. That flags it for a longer test, which should stop it coming straight back to you unfixed.

Exchange 2 — Booking a dentist
M: The earliest routine appointment I have with Dr Osborne is the fourteenth, I'm afraid.
W: The fourteenth. That's nearly three weeks. It isn't agony, exactly — it's more of a dull ache that flares up whenever I drink anything cold.
M: If it were constant I'd class it as urgent and squeeze you in tomorrow morning. As it stands, what I can do is put you on the cancellation list. People do drop out, though it's usually at very short notice.
W: Put me down, then. I'll take whatever comes, even if you ring me at half past eight and want me there at nine.

Exchange 3 — Negotiating a deadline with a tutor
W: So you're asking for an extension on the literature review.
M: Ten days, if that's at all possible. Two of my sources only arrived last week from the archive, and — honestly — I underestimated how long the coding would take.
W: Let me be straight with you. I can approve five days myself, no paperwork, no questions. Ten means a formal mitigating-circumstances claim, and the panel tends to want documentation that, from what you've told me, you probably don't have.
M: Five it is, then. I'd rather have something certain than gamble on a committee and lose three weeks finding out.

Exchange 4 — Gym induction
M: So the induction covers all the machines, but between you and me, the machines are the least of it.
W: Meaning what, exactly?
M: Meaning the people who disappear in February don't disappear because they can't operate a rowing machine. They disappear because they came four times a week for a fortnight and then their knees told them exactly what they thought of that.
W: So what you're saying is, start slower than I want to.
M: I'm saying start slower than you think is even worth doing. Twice a week, for a month. Then come and find me and we'll talk about adding a third.

Exchange 5 — Reporting a lost passport
W: And you're certain it was lost rather than stolen?
M: Certain isn't the word I'd use. I last had it at the station, and I've been through the bag twice — but nothing else is missing, no cards, no cash, which is really why I haven't bothered the police with it.
W: I'd go anyway. Not because we insist on it — we don't, for the emergency document — but because if that passport surfaces somewhere it shouldn't in six months' time, a report dated today is the thing that protects you.
M: That genuinely hadn't occurred to me. Where's the nearest station?

Exchange 6 — Arranging a house move
M: We can do the thirtieth, but I'll be honest with you: it's the last Friday of the month and on those days everything takes longer. Traffic, lifts, other crews in the same building.
W: My tenancy ends on the thirty-first, so it's the thirtieth or nothing.
M: Then take the eight o'clock slot rather than the midday one. It costs exactly the same. The difference is that by midday we're already running an hour behind somebody else's move, and you spend your afternoon watching two men apologise.
W: Eight, then. I'll set two alarms.

Exchange 7 — Choosing a phone plan
W: The unlimited plan is twelve pounds more a month, and I'll tell you now, nine out of ten customers who take it don't come anywhere near using it.
M: But the cheaper one has that data cap, and if I go over it —
W: You're charged, yes. But you'd have to go over by a fair amount, month after month, before it added up to twelve pounds. Look, I'm not trying to talk you out of it. I'm saying pay the twelve pounds if you want to stop thinking about it — not because it'll save you money, because it won't.
M: Fair enough. On reflection, I think I'd quite like to stop thinking about it.

Exchange 8 — Complaining about noise
M: It's the third night this week. I'm not asking for anyone to be thrown out — I'd just like to sleep.
W: I understand. Have you spoken to them directly at all?
M: Twice. And both times they were perfectly pleasant, apologised, said it wouldn't happen again. That's rather the problem, isn't it. If they'd been rude about it I'd at least know where I stood.
W: Then I'll write to them formally. It creates a record, and having a record on file is what makes the next conversation a different sort of conversation.

parts.instructionsEn: You will hear two monologues. Complete the notes. Write NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS for each answer.

context.transcript:
PART 2 — TWO MONOLOGUES

Monologue A — Museum audio guide, stop seven

Welcome to stop seven of the audio guide: the Whitcombe Gallery. Now, almost every visitor assumes that the collection in this room was assembled by Sir Henry Whitcombe himself. In fact — and this is far and away the commonest misconception about the house — the greater part of it was bought by his daughter, Eleanor, who inherited both the estate and, rather more significantly, its debts. Instead of selling, which is what everyone expected her to do, she began buying, and by 1904 the gallery held over four hundred works.

The room you're standing in wasn't built as a gallery at all. It was the stables until 1912, which explains two things you may already have noticed: the unusually high ceiling, and the fact that all the windows face north. That last point was deliberate rather than accidental. North light doesn't shift as the day goes on, so the paintings are seen in more or less the same conditions at ten in the morning and four in the afternoon.

One word of warning before you move on. The large seascape on your right is a copy — a very good one, but a copy. The original was sold in 1936 to pay for the roof, and although the family always maintained they would buy it back, it hangs today in Melbourne. Photography without flash is permitted throughout the house, with one exception: the small side room containing the watercolours. Those fade, and they don't come back.

Monologue B — Conference registration announcement

Good morning, everybody, and welcome to the Institute. Just a few practical words about registration before we go through to the opening plenary.

Your badge is in an envelope with your name on it, and you'll find those at desk B. Not desk A, despite what it says in your printed programme — desk A is for speakers only. The programme went to print before that arrangement changed, and I'm afraid we didn't catch it.

Lunch is included in your fee, but you will need the blue voucher, and the voucher is not in the envelope. You collect it at the door of the dining hall, and you can only collect it once, so please don't put it down somewhere and forget about it.

If you've booked the Thursday excursion, do note that the coach leaves from the rear car park, not from the main entrance where it stopped last year, and it leaves at half past eight sharp. And finally, the wifi password has changed since the pre-conference email went out. It is now harbour2026 — all one word, lower case, no space, no capital letter.

parts.titleEn: Part 3: Two researchers discuss their survey (Questions 15-18)
parts.instructionsUz: Ikki tadqiqotchining suhbatini eshitasiz. To'g'ri javobni tanlang. Ular bir-birining fikriga qisman qo'shiladi — kim nimani aytayotganiga diqqat qiling.
parts.instructionsEn: Listen to two researchers discussing a survey. Choose the correct answer. They partly agree with each other: pay attention to who says what.

context.transcript:
PART 3 — TWO RESEARCHERS DISCUSSING A SURVEY

W: Right. Headline finding first: sixty-eight per cent said they would accept a pay cut in exchange for flexible hours.
M: Which is the number everyone will quote on Friday, and it happens to be the number I trust least in the whole dataset.
W: Go on.
M: Because we asked it in the abstract. "Would you accept less money for more flexibility?" Well, of course people say yes — it costs nothing to say yes. When we put an actual figure in the follow-up item, and I mean a concrete one, eight per cent of gross salary, the proportion collapsed to nineteen.
W: That's fair, and I'm not disputing the arithmetic. But I'd argue the abstract question still tells us something real. It measures how people want to see themselves — the sort of worker they'd like to be. That isn't nothing. It predicts, fairly well, what they'll say to their employer in a performance review.
M: It predicts what they'll say. It doesn't predict what they'll sign.
W: No. Agreed. Although my real worry is somewhere else entirely, if I'm honest. Our sample skewed badly towards people who were already working remotely. We recruited through professional networks because it was cheap and it was fast, and we've paid for that in representativeness.
M: We did flag it.
W: We flagged it in a footnote on page forty-one. If the press release doesn't put it in the first paragraph, nobody will ever read it — and then in eighteen months somebody replicates us properly, gets a different number, and it's our credibility that takes the damage, not theirs. That's what I want changed before Friday.
M: Fine. Put it up front, I've no objection. Though I'd rather we didn't oversell the caveat either. The direction of the finding is almost certainly right, even if the magnitude isn't, and if we hedge every sentence nobody takes anything away from it at all.
W: Nobody's suggesting we bury the finding. Just say the limitation earlier, and say it plainly.
M: I can live with that.

parts.instructionsUz: Avtomobilsiz shahar markazlari haqidagi intervyuni eshitasiz. To'g'ri javobni tanlang.
parts.instructionsEn: Listen to an interview about car-free city centres and choose the correct answer.

context.transcript:
PART 4 — INTERVIEW WITH AN URBAN PLANNER

W: Dr Alvi, you've advised four cities on pedestrianisation over the last decade. Is the car-free city centre an idea whose time has finally come?
M: It's an idea whose slogan has come, which isn't at all the same thing. "Car-free" is a wonderful phrase and a fairly terrible policy description, because almost nowhere is genuinely car-free. Deliveries still happen. Disabled residents drive. Ambulances exist. What we're actually talking about, in every scheme I've ever worked on, is reallocating road space from one use to another — and I accept that's a duller sentence, but it's the honest one.
W: Does the terminology really matter that much?
M: It matters enormously, because it determines who lines up against you before you've said anything else. Tell a shopkeeper the centre is going car-free and what he hears is "my customers can no longer reach me". Tell him instead that you're widening the pavement outside his door and removing eleven parking spaces on a street where the average parked car belongs to an office worker rather than a customer — and now you're having a completely different conversation. A factual one. And a factual conversation is one you can actually win.
W: And can you win it? The evidence on retail impact is, after all, contested.
M: Contested is fair, I won't pretend otherwise. What I'd say is that the evidence is reasonably good but the timeline is brutal. Footfall typically rises within, oh, eighteen months to two years. The difficulty is that traders don't experience eighteen months, they experience the first six — and the first six months are roadworks, dust and a hoarding across the front of the shop. Several perfectly sound schemes have been reversed by councils that were, in effect, judging a two-year policy on the basis of a six-month sample.
W: So the failures are political rather than technical.
M: Mostly, yes. Although I'd resist letting my own profession off quite that easily. We have been guilty, repeatedly, of designing very beautiful squares that nobody has the slightest reason to cross. If you close a street and put nothing in it — no market, no seating, no shade, no reason to linger — then you haven't created public space at all. You've created a gap. And the public notices the difference immediately, even if the awards jury doesn't.
W: If you could change one thing about the way these schemes are introduced, what would it be?
M: Do the boring part first. Before you lift a single paving stone, fix the bus frequency. Every scheme I've watched succeed had a transport alternative running properly, and visibly, six months before any restriction came in. Every scheme I've watched fail did it in the opposite order — imposed the restriction and then asked the public to have faith that the alternative would arrive. It's not a technical failing. It's an impatience problem.

parts.titleEn: Part 5: A career adviser on changing careers after 30 (Questions 24-29)
parts.instructionsUz: Monologni eshitib, gaplarni to'ldiring. Har bir javob 1-3 so'zdan iborat bo'lishi kerak.
parts.instructionsEn: Listen to the talk and complete the sentences. Write NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS for each answer.

context.transcript:
PART 5 — CAREER ADVISER: CHANGING CAREERS AFTER THIRTY

Thank you. I want to talk about changing career after thirty, and I want to begin by dismantling the single most common piece of advice you will ever hear on the subject, which is "follow your passion". In fifteen years of advising people I have almost never seen that work as a starting point. It works beautifully as a description of where people eventually end up, and it works terribly as a method for getting there. Passion, in my experience, is far more often a consequence of competence than a cause of it. You get good at something, and then you love it. Very rarely the other way round.

So what does work? Three things, and I'm afraid none of them is glamorous.

The first is what I'd call the sideways step. People imagine a career change as a leap: you resign on Friday as an accountant and reappear on Monday as a graphic designer. The changes that actually succeed are almost always partial. You change either the industry or the function — but not both at once. Change both simultaneously and you throw away every scrap of leverage you have, and you find yourself competing against twenty-two-year-olds on their terms, which is a competition you will lose.

The second is evidence. Not enthusiasm — evidence. Before you spend money on retraining you need proof that you can do the work, and, much more importantly, proof that you can stand doing it on a wet Tuesday afternoon in February when nobody is watching. So take on one small paid project, however badly paid it is, before you commit to anything larger. Roughly a third of the people who sit in that chair discover at exactly that stage that what they wanted was the identity, not the job. That is not a failure. That is thirty thousand pounds saved.

The third is money, and here I'm going to be blunt with you. The realistic figure — and I've seen enough of these to be reasonably confident — is that you should expect your income to dip for about two years. Not two months. Two years. If your finances cannot absorb that, the plan isn't wrong, but the timing is, and what you need is a longer runway, not a braver decision.

One last thing, and then questions. Age is a smaller obstacle than most people believe, but it does change the argument you have to make. At twenty-five you are hired for your potential. At thirty-eight you are hired for your judgement — so stop apologising for the years you spent somewhere else and start pricing them properly. Those years are not baggage. They are the only asset you hold that the twenty-two-year-old cannot possibly have.

parts.titleEn: Part 6: University lecture on the psychology of habit formation (Questions 30-35)
parts.instructionsUz: Ma'ruzani eshiting va to'g'ri javobni tanlang. Ma'ruzachi qayerda dalilga, qayerda o'z fikriga tayanayotganiga e'tibor bering.
parts.instructionsEn: Listen to the lecture and choose the correct answer. Note where the lecturer relies on evidence and where on his own opinion.

context.transcript:
PART 6 — UNIVERSITY LECTURE: THE PSYCHOLOGY OF HABIT FORMATION

Right, let's begin. Today, habit formation — and I want to spend most of this hour explaining why the popular account of it is wrong. Or rather, not wrong exactly, so much as wildly oversimplified in a way that has practical consequences.

You will all have encountered the claim that it takes twenty-one days to form a habit. That figure comes, indirectly, from a plastic surgeon writing in the nineteen-sixties about how long his patients took to adjust psychologically to their new appearance. It was, in essence, an observation about adjustment and grief, and it has been repeated ever since as though it were the result of a controlled experiment. It isn't. When Lally and colleagues actually went out and measured it in 2009, the median was sixty-six days — and this is the part that invariably gets left out of the magazine version — the range ran from eighteen days at one end to two hundred and fifty-four at the other. So the honest answer to "how long does it take?" is: it depends enormously, and it depends mostly on the behaviour rather than on you. Drinking a glass of water after breakfast automates very quickly indeed. Fifty sit-ups does not, and no amount of character will change that.

Now, the mechanism. The standard model is cue, routine, reward, and I'd defend it as far as it goes. A habit is a learned association between a context and a response, and what shifts as the habit matures is not that you want the reward more. Quite the opposite, in fact. Once a behaviour is genuinely habitual, the reward matters less than it did at the beginning. This has been demonstrated fairly convincingly in the animal work: over-train a behaviour, then devalue the reward — make the food less appealing, or pair it with mild illness — and the animal carries on performing the behaviour anyway. Which tells us something rather uncomfortable, namely that mature habits are relatively insensitive to whether they are still doing us any good at all.

Which brings me to the practical implication — and here I want to be clear that I'm going somewhat beyond the strict evidence, so treat what follows as informed opinion rather than established finding. If habits are fundamentally context-driven, then the highest-leverage intervention available to you is not willpower. It's moving. Changing your environment, your route to work, the layout of your kitchen. The studies of people who relocate suggest that this is precisely when habits are most plastic — you get a window of a few weeks in which the old cues simply aren't there to trigger the old responses. And most people waste that window completely, because they're busy unpacking boxes.

One caveat before we finish, and it's an important one. Almost everything I've described this hour concerns the formation of simple, repeated, voluntary behaviours. Whether the same account extends to the persistence of, say, addiction is genuinely disputed within the field, and anyone who assures you that question has been settled is, I'd suggest, selling you something.

parts.passageText:
Why cities are rethinking the office

A. The vacancy figures, striking as they are, understate what has actually happened. Occupancy — the proportion of desks in use on an ordinary Tuesday — has fallen further and faster than the leasing data suggests, because companies have gone on paying for floors they no longer fill, waiting patiently for agreements signed in a quite different decade to run their course. The reckoning, in other words, has been deferred rather than avoided, and the deferral has flattered every quarterly report published since.

B. What draws people back, where anything does, is rarely the desk itself. Surveys of returning staff place collaboration, mentoring and what one respondent memorably called "overhearing" at the top of the list — the incidental learning that occurs when a junior colleague half-listens to a senior one handling a difficult client. Firms that have succeeded in filling their buildings have generally done so by making them worth the journey rather than by issuing instructions about attendance, which tend to be complied with narrowly and resented broadly.

C. Conversion is the obvious answer and by some distance the hardest one. A tower built in the 1970s typically has a floor plate too deep for residential use: bedrooms require windows, and the middle of such a building is a very long way from one. Add to that plumbing risers sized for two lavatories per floor rather than forty bathrooms, and the arithmetic that looks so persuasive in a newspaper column has a habit of collapsing in a structural engineer's spreadsheet.

D. The consequences reach a good deal further than landlords and their lenders. The sandwich shop, the dry cleaner and the bus route were all sized for a population that turned up five days a week. Municipal budgets, too, lean heavily on commercial property taxes; a number of American cities now face a shortfall in precisely the revenue that funds the services — transit, policing, street cleaning — which make a downtown worth travelling to in the first place.

E. Not every city is experiencing the same shock, and the pattern of who suffers is instructive. Districts laid out before the car, with narrow streets, mixed uses and flats above the shops, have proved noticeably more resilient than purpose-built financial quarters, which empty at six o'clock by design rather than by accident. The lesson is arguably less about remote work than about monoculture: a district that does one thing is fragile the moment that one thing changes.

F. Where reinvention has worked, it has usually been slow, subsidised and thoroughly unglamorous — tax abatements, relaxed zoning, a university faculty persuaded to take three floors on a long lease. Officials hoping for a single transformative project would do better to study the cities that spent a decade making a hundred small permissions marginally easier to obtain. That is not a policy that attracts ribbon-cutting or photographers, but it appears, on the available evidence, to be the one that works.

parts.titleEn: Part 2: The science of sleep debt (Questions 7-14)
parts.instructionsEn: Read the text and answer questions 7-14.
parts.passageText:
The science of sleep debt

The metaphor of debt is seductive and, like most seductive metaphors, only partly accurate. It implies a ledger: lose two hours on Monday, repay them on Saturday, return to zero. Two decades of research suggest something a good deal less tidy. Some of what is lost can indeed be recovered, some of it apparently cannot, and the body proves markedly worse at settling the account than the metaphor leads us to expect.

The clearest demonstration remains a set of laboratory studies in which volunteers were restricted to six hours in bed for two consecutive weeks. Their performance on tests of sustained attention declined steadily throughout, and by the end of the fortnight it was comparable to that of people who had gone entirely without sleep for two nights. What made the finding genuinely unsettling, however, was not the impairment itself but the participants' assessment of it. Their subjective ratings of sleepiness plateaued after only a few days, while their objective performance carried on deteriorating. They felt, in short, that they had adapted. They had not. They had merely lost the capacity to notice that they hadn't.

Recovery is possible but asymmetric. A single long weekend restores alertness to something close to baseline on most measures, which is precisely why the practice of sleeping late at weekends persists: it works, up to a point. Metabolic markers, however, appear to be considerably more stubborn. In one frequently cited trial, participants whose alertness had returned after a weekend of extended sleep nonetheless showed insulin sensitivity that had not come back to its starting value, and the mismatch widened when the cycle of restriction and catch-up was repeated over several weeks. The uncomfortable implication is that feeling restored and being restored are separable states.

There is also the prior question of what counts as debt at all. Individual sleep need is more variable than public-health messaging tends to admit; the familiar eight-hour figure is a population average, and a genuine minority of adults function well on appreciably less with no measurable cost. The difficulty is that self-assessment is least reliable in exactly those people who most confidently claim to need the least. Researchers who have brought self-described short sleepers into the laboratory typically find that a large majority of them perform like everybody else — that is to say, badly — once they are deprived under controlled conditions.

What, then, is the practical advice? Sleep researchers are usually rather more modest than the popular literature written about them. Regularity of timing, they suggest, may matter as much as total duration: going to bed and waking at consistent hours produces better outcomes across several cohort studies than simply adding hours on an erratic schedule. Beyond that, the honest position is that the mechanisms linking chronic short sleep to cardiovascular and metabolic disease are well established as associations and remain, in several important respects, incompletely explained.

parts.passageText:
How a small country reformed its schools

Thirty years ago the country's schools were unremarkable by any international measure. Today they are visited by delegations from four continents. [15] ____________ That story, however, is told a great deal more often than it is understood, and the details that get omitted in the telling are usually the ones that matter.

The reform did not begin in the classroom. It began in the universities. [16] ____________ The consequence was that within a decade teaching had become a genuinely competitive profession: places on training courses were harder to obtain than places in law, and applicants who were turned away did not simply apply somewhere else, because there was nowhere else to apply.

Curiously, the reform involved doing rather less of several things that other systems were busy doing more of. National testing was reduced rather than expanded. [17] ____________ Inspectors were withdrawn altogether, and the money saved was redirected into the professional development of the teachers who remained.

Critics predicted at the time that standards would fall in the absence of external monitoring. [18] ____________ What replaced inspection was not nothing, but it was something considerably harder to export: a dense set of professional norms, sustained by the fact that every adult in the staffroom had been through the same demanding training and could be assumed to have.

The results, when they eventually arrived, were widely misread. [19] ____________ Commentators concentrated almost exclusively on the country's average score, which was indeed high; the more remarkable figure was the unusually narrow gap between its strongest and weakest schools — a measure of equity rather than of excellence.

Attempts to copy the model abroad have had decidedly mixed success. [20] ____________ The obvious explanation is that visiting officials tend to import the visible features — shorter days, later starting ages, fewer examinations — while leaving behind the invisible one, which took fifteen years and a good deal of political courage to construct.

There is also a less comfortable possibility, which the country's own researchers raise more readily than its admirers do. [21] ____________ Whether a reform that depended on a small, wealthy and socially cohesive population can be reproduced in larger and more divided societies remains, after three decades of admiring visits, an entirely open question.

parts.instructionsUz: Muallifning munosabati va bilvosita xulosalariga e'tibor bering. Ba'zi variantlar matnda aytilgan, lekin savolga javob bermaydi.
parts.instructionsEn: Pay attention to the writer's attitude and implied meaning. Some options are stated in the text but do not answer the question.
parts.passageText:
Is remote work widening inequality?

There is a version of the remote-work story in which everybody wins, and it is worth stating plainly before taking it apart. In this account the office was always a somewhat arbitrary constraint; freed from it, workers reclaim their commuting hours, firms recruit from a far wider pool, and prosperity finally leaks out of the expensive cities and into the towns that have spent forty years watching their graduates leave. Some of this has genuinely happened. That is precisely what makes the rest of the argument difficult, and why the sceptics who dismiss the whole thing as a fad are no more persuasive than the enthusiasts.

Begin with who is eligible. Roughly a third of jobs in advanced economies can be performed from home, and that third is not distributed at random. It is concentrated among the highly educated, the well paid and the already secure. The nurse, the warehouse picker and the bus driver did not gain two hours a day; a good number of them gained a manager who now supervises them by video and understands their work rather less well than before. To describe as a universal liberation a benefit flowing overwhelmingly to the top third of the income distribution requires a certain agility.

Even within the eligible group the gains are unevenly claimed. Early evidence suggests that the employees most likely to be at home five days a week are those with the least bargaining power in their organisations, while those most reliably present on the days that matter are the ones already marked out for advancement. If physical proximity to decision-makers continues to influence promotion — and there is very little sign that it has stopped doing so — then a norm of flexible attendance may quietly harden into a two-tier workforce, the visible on one track and the invisible on another. The mechanism here is not malice. It is the ordinary, unremarkable tendency of managers to think first of the people they have seen most recently.

The geographical argument deserves rather more sympathy than it usually receives from urbanists. House prices in a number of mid-sized towns have risen sharply, which is unwelcome news for the people who already lived there and excellent news for nobody in particular; but local spending has risen too, and several of these places are demonstrably livelier than they were a decade ago. Whether this amounts to a transfer of prosperity or merely to its redistribution within the same professional class is the real question, and the honest answer is that it is still too early to say. What can be said with confidence is that the towns doing best are not the cheapest ones. They are the ones with a station.

None of this makes remote work a mistake. The commuting hours were real, the carbon savings are real, and for parents and disabled workers the change has been transformative in a way that decades of well-meaning policy conspicuously failed to achieve. The point being made here is narrower. A reform that helps a third of workers substantially and the remainder not at all is, by definition, a widening of the distance between them, however welcome its effects on those it does reach. Calling that progress is entirely defensible. Calling it inclusion is not.

parts.titleEn: Part 5: Academic text — Language death and what is lost with it (Questions 29-35)
parts.instructionsUz: Matnni o'qing. Ba'zi savollarga variantlardan tanlab, ba'zilariga esa matndan olingan 1-3 so'z bilan javob bering.
parts.instructionsEn: Read the text. Answer some questions by choosing an option and others with NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS from the text.
parts.passageText:
Language death and what is lost with it

Of the roughly seven thousand languages currently spoken, a widely cited estimate holds that between half and ninety per cent will have ceased to be spoken by the end of this century. The sheer width of that interval is itself informative: it reflects genuine disagreement about what counts as a distinct language, what counts as a speaker, and at what point a language should be described as dead rather than merely dormant. Linguists distinguish, for example, between a language that has lost its last fluent speaker and one that retains a community of partial speakers who understand it but no longer produce it — a state that has occasionally proved reversible, though only under conditions that are difficult to engineer deliberately.

The mechanism of loss is rarely dramatic. Languages are seldom banned outright, though that has certainly happened; far more often they are abandoned, in a sequence remarkably consistent across continents. A community becomes bilingual, typically for economic reasons. Parents, acting rationally and often at considerable emotional cost, begin speaking the majority language to their children in the belief — usually a correct one — that it will improve their prospects. Within two generations the ancestral language is confined to ceremony and to the elderly. Fishman's model of graded intergenerational disruption describes this progression in eight stages, and its central claim is that the decisive threshold is intergenerational transmission: once children stop acquiring a language in the home, formal instruction on its own has almost never proved sufficient to reverse the decline.

What, precisely, is lost? The strongest version of the argument — that each language encodes a unique worldview, and that its disappearance therefore diminishes the range of human thought itself — rests on a linguistic relativity hypothesis that most contemporary researchers regard as, at best, weakly supported. Grammatical structure appears to influence cognition at the margins rather than to determine it. Advocates of documentation have accordingly shifted their emphasis, and the contemporary case is now made on narrower but distinctly firmer ground.

Three claims survive scrutiny reasonably well. The first is empirical: linguistic diversity constitutes the evidence base for the science of language itself, and a theory of what human grammars are capable of is only as good as the sample on which it was built. Rare structures — evidentials, which oblige a speaker to mark how they know what they assert, or numeral systems with no exact word for four — are disproportionately found in small and endangered languages. The second is ecological: a great deal of traditional knowledge concerning local species, seasonal patterns and medicinal plants exists only in oral form and is not straightforwardly translatable, since the underlying taxonomies themselves differ from those of the incoming language. The third claim is social, and is arguably the most important: communities that have undergone language shift report consequences for wellbeing and cohesion that are hard to quantify but harder still to dismiss, and revitalisation programmes in several countries have been associated with measurable improvements in educational attainment and, in at least one much-discussed study, with reduced rates of youth suicide.

Revitalisation, where it has worked at all, has depended a good deal less on technology than its enthusiasts assume. Digital archives preserve records; they do not create speakers. The cases usually held up as successes — Hebrew, Welsh, Maori — share a rather different feature: in each, a domain existed in which the language became necessary rather than merely available, whether the state, the school or the workplace. Necessity, not sentiment, appears to be the operative variable, which is an uncomfortable conclusion for campaigns built on affection alone.

options: It remains the strongest case for preservation
It depends on a hypothesis that is only weakly supported

sections.instructionsUz: Uchala vazifani ham bajaring. Tavsiya etilgan vaqt: Task 1 — 10 daqiqa, Task 2 — 20 daqiqa, Task 3 — 30 daqiqa. So'z sonidan kam yozsangiz ball pasayadi. C1 darajasida uslub (registr) mosligi, murakkab grammatika va aniq leksika alohida baholanadi.
sections.instructionsEn: Complete all three tasks. Suggested timing: Task 1 — 10 minutes, Task 2 — 20 minutes, Task 3 — 30 minutes. At C1 level, register control, complex structures and precise lexis are assessed explicitly.

parts.instructionsUz: Ikkita xat yozing: birinchisi norasmiy, ikkinchisi rasmiy uslubda. Uslublar farqiga alohida e'tibor bering.
parts.instructionsEn: Write two emails: the first informal, the second formal. Register control is assessed.

questions.promptEn:
You have received this email from your friend Dilnoza:

"Hi! I need to think out loud at someone, and you're the person whose judgement I trust. I've been offered a two-year contract in Warsaw — better money, better title, but I'd be leaving my parents, my flat and basically everyone I know. Part of me thinks I'd regret not going. Part of me thinks I'm romanticising it. Would you go? What would worry you most? And be honest — you're the only person who hasn't just told me what I want to hear. Dilnoza"

Write a reply to Dilnoza. Answer all three of her questions and give her a clear recommendation. Write at least 50 words.
questions.promptUz: Do'stingiz Dilnozadan xat keldi (yuqorida): unga Varshavada ikki yillik shartnoma taklif qilishgan, lekin u ikkilanmoqda. Javob xat yozing: uning uchala savoliga ham javob bering va aniq maslahat bering. Kamida 50 so'z. Norasmiy uslub.

rubric.style: informal email to a close friend: contractions, phrasal verbs, direct address, personal tone; all three questions answered plus a clear recommendation
formal business email: appropriate salutation and sign-off, no contractions, hedged and diplomatic phrasing, all four content points covered within 120-150 words

parts.instructionsUz: Ikkala qarashni ham muhokama qiling va o'z fikringizni aniq bildiring. Kamida 250 so'z.
parts.instructionsEn: Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.

questions.promptEn:
Write an essay on the following topic:

"Some argue that governments should prioritise economic growth over environmental protection. Others believe the opposite. Discuss both views and give your own opinion."

Support your argument with reasons and relevant examples. Write at least 250 words.
questions.promptUz:
Quyidagi mavzuda esse yozing:

«Ba'zilar hukumatlar atrof-muhitni muhofaza qilishdan ko'ra iqtisodiy o'sishni ustuvor qilishi kerak deb hisoblaydi. Boshqalar esa aksincha fikrda. Ikkala qarashni ham muhokama qiling va o'z fikringizni bildiring.»

Fikringizni sabab va misollar bilan asoslang. Kamida 250 so'z.

rubric.style: formal discursive essay: both views developed with reasons and examples, a clearly stated and consistently maintained personal position, paragraphing with a distinct introduction and conclusion, and C1 features such as hedging, concession and nominalisation

sections.instructionsUz: Uchta qismda mikrofonga javob yozib qoldiring. Tayyorgarlik vaqti tugagach yozuv avtomatik boshlanadi. AI javobingizni transkripsiya qilib, rasmiy mezonlar bo'yicha baholaydi va o'zbekcha tahlil beradi.
sections.instructionsEn: Record your answer for each of the three parts. Recording starts automatically when preparation time ends.

parts.titleEn: Part 1: Work, study and free time (B1-B2)
parts.instructionsUz: Tayyorgarlik 10 soniya, javob 60 soniya. Har bir savolga javob berishga harakat qiling.
parts.instructionsEn: 10 seconds to prepare, 60 seconds to speak. Try to address every question.

questions.promptEn: Let's talk about your work or studies and your free time. What do you do at the moment — do you work or are you a student? What is the most interesting part of it, and what is the least? And when you finish for the day, how do you usually switch off?
questions.promptUz: Ish yoki o'qishingiz va bo'sh vaqtingiz haqida gaplashamiz. Hozir nima bilan shug'ullanasiz — ishlaysizmi yoki o'qiysizmi? Undagi eng qiziqarli va eng zerikarli jihat nima? Kun tugagach, odatda qanday dam olasiz?

rubric.level: B1-B2: answers all parts of the question, extends beyond one-sentence replies, uses a range of present and past tenses accurately

parts.titleEn: Part 2: Individual long turn — lifelong learning (B2-C1)
parts.instructionsUz: Tayyorgarlik 60 soniya, javob 120 soniya. Ijobiy va salbiy tomonlarni muvozanatli yoriting, so'ng o'z tanlovingizni aytib, asoslang.
parts.instructionsEn: 60 seconds to prepare, 120 seconds to speak. Balance advantages and disadvantages, then state and justify your own choice.

questions.promptEn: More and more adults are returning to study in their thirties, forties and beyond — retraining, taking online courses, or doing a second degree. Describe the advantages and disadvantages of continuing to learn formally throughout your working life. Then say what you personally would choose: to keep retraining every few years, or to build deep expertise in one field and stay there. Explain your reasoning.
questions.promptUz: Tobora ko'proq kattalar 30, 40 va undan keyingi yoshda yana o'qishga qaytmoqda — qayta tayyorlanish, onlayn kurslar yoki ikkinchi oliy ta'lim. Butun mehnat faoliyati davomida rasmiy o'qishni davom ettirishning afzalliklari va kamchiliklarini tasvirlab bering. So'ng siz shaxsan nimani tanlashingizni ayting: har necha yilda qayta o'qishnimi yoki bitta sohada chuqur mutaxassis bo'lib qolishnimi. Sababini tushuntiring.

rubric.level: B2-C1: clearly structured long turn, both sides covered before the personal choice, topic-specific lexis (retraining, obsolescence, transferable skills), accurate conditionals and comparison

parts.instructionsUz: Tayyorgarlik 60 soniya, javob 120 soniya. Ikkala tomonni ham ko'rib chiqing, qarama-qarshi dalilni tan oling va aniq xulosaga keling.
parts.instructionsEn: 60 seconds to prepare, 120 seconds to speak. Address both sides, concede a counter-argument, and reach a clear conclusion.

questions.promptEn: "Technology has made us more connected but less close." Discuss both sides of this statement. Consider what digital communication has genuinely made possible, as well as what it may have replaced or weakened, and make it clear where you finally stand and why.
questions.promptUz: «Texnologiya bizni ko'proq bog'lab qo'ydi, lekin bir-birimizga yaqinligimizni kamaytirdi». Bu fikrning ikkala tomonini ham muhokama qiling. Raqamli muloqot haqiqatan nimani mumkin qilganini va nimaning o'rnini egallab, nimani zaiflashtirgan bo'lishi mumkinligini ko'rib chiqing, so'ng o'z pozitsiyangizni aniq bildiring va asoslang.

rubric.level: C1: sustained abstract argument, explicit concession and rebuttal, precise and idiomatic lexis, wide grammatical range with only occasional slips, natural stress and intonation
